metadata.title: Hierarchical clustering of the pre-exam anxiety levels in physically inactive and active adolescent students from 56 countries: an observational study using PISA program data
metadata.venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 data (56 countries) and aggregates pre-exam anxiety information to country-level mean percentages for two physical-activity groups (low vs high/moderate-vigorous). The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling/survey weights (e.g., student design weights) or any replicate-weight variance estimation, and it also states that raw microdata were not accessed. Because the analysis is performed on country-level averages and then clustered using Euclidean distances, the paper does not describe any complex-survey-weighted estimation procedure. Analysts replicating this work should use the PISA 2018 sampling weights when computing country-level anxiety percentages from microdata, and should document whether clustering is performed on weighted country estimates or unweighted means.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is not a PV-based cognitive achievement score; instead, the study uses pre-exam anxiety levels summarized as country-level mean percentages for students in two physical-activity categories. Plausible Values are typically generated for cognitive achievement domains in PISA, whereas this paper’s outcome is an affective measure aggregated for clustering, so PV handling is not applicable by design. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data procedure for the anxiety or physical-activity variables used to compute the country-level percentages, so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PISA 2018 data for 15-year-old students across 56 countries, but the authors state they did not have access to the raw dataset. They construct two clustering datasets by physical-activity status: (1) students who do not engage in any regular physical activity (low physical activity) and (2) students who regularly engage in moderate to vigorous physical activities (high physical activity). For each physical-activity group, pre-exam anxiety is encoded as a numeric continuous variable and then aggregated to country-level mean percentage anxiety rates, with each country treated as an individual observation for hierarchical clustering. The paper does not report additional grade/school-type filters beyond the PISA 2018 target age group, nor does it specify any explicit missing-data exclusion or imputation rule for the anxiety or physical-activity variables used to compute the country-level percentages.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 data for 15-year-old students across 56 c, the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This observational study uses PISA 2018 (15-year-old students) from 56 countries to examine pre-exam anxiety patterns separately for two habitual physical-activity groups: physically inactive (no regular activity) and physically active (moderate-to-vigorous activity). Because the authors do not access microdata, they cluster countries using country-level mean percentages of pre-exam anxiety for each physical-activity group, treating each country as one data point. The hierarchical clustering quality is evaluated with silhouette score (0.60 for the low-activity clustering with five clusters; 0.56 for the high-activity clustering with four clusters), within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), between-cluster sum of squares (BCSS), explained variation (96% for low activity; 92% for high activity), and BCSS/WCSS ratios (22.10 and 11.18). The paper reports statistically significant within-country differences in anxiety between activity groups for multiple countries (e.g., Austria, Belgium, Chile, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Israel, Korea, Mexico, Turkey, United States), while Russia and the UAE show increases. Limitations include lack of reported missing-data handling, lack of documented survey-weighted estimation for country means, and the fact that clustering is descriptive rather than a predictive model of individual anxiety. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The study is an exploratory clustering analysis rather than a supervised ML prediction task, so no predictive target-variable modeling is reported and therefore no ML algorithm performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) are applicable in the schema’s predictive sense. The paper also does not report plausible-values or missing-data handling because the outcome is an affective measure summarized as country-level anxiety percentages for clustering, and the authors explicitly state they did not access raw microdata. As a result, fields related to predictive ML techniques and PV/missing-data transparency are necessarily sparse.
